## Welcome {.unnumbered}

Last class you built a pair of weighted dice. Today you are going to do
something you have **not** been taught how to do --- and you are going to do it
in about fifteen minutes, with a colleague, using an LLM as your second pair of hands.

The point of this session is not that the LLM can write code for you, but that *how you ask* determines whether you get
something correct or something plausible, and that telling those two apart is
your job, not the model's.

## Large Language Models 

How LLMs work and what they can and cannot do deserve far more time than what we have in this section. In the meantime, I encourage you to familiarize yourself with some of the foundational literature on these topics. Here are two recommendations to get started:

- Bender, E. M., Gebru, T., McMillan-Major, A., & Shmitchell, S. (2021).
  [On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots: Can Language Models Be Too Big? 🦜](https://doi.org/10.1145/3442188.3445922)
  *Proceedings of the 2021 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and
  Transparency (FAccT '21)*, 610–623.

- Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. (2026).
  [Chapter 1: Introduction](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/1.pdf).
  In *Speech and Language Processing* (3rd ed. draft, August 19, 2026).

- Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. (2026).
  [Chapter 2: Words and Tokens](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/2.pdf).
  In *Speech and Language Processing* (3rd ed. draft, August 19, 2026).


::: {.callout-note}
## How this hands-on exercise works

Keep **two tabs open**: this page, and whatever LLM you use (ChatGPT, Claude,
Gemini, etc.).

Every grey box below is a real R console running inside your browser. Paste the
code the LLM gives you into the box, click **Run Code**, and compare what you
get to the target. 

The first box takes a few seconds to wake up while R loads and the dataset
uploads. Start it now, before you read on.
:::

::: {.rule}
**The one rule for today.**

You must be able to say **what the code should do** before you ask, and check
**that it did that** after.

Everything below is built to make you do both. If you get the right number
without being able to say why it is right, you have not finished the problem.
:::

## The data {.unnumbered}

`voting.csv` comes from a real experiment --- Gerber, Green and Larimer (2008).
Before the 2006 Michigan primary, researchers mailed some registered voters a
letter showing **whether their neighbours had voted** in past elections. Then
they recorded who actually turned out.

It has 229,444 rows and three columns:

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `birth` | Year of birth |
| `message` | `"yes"` if the household got the social-pressure mailing, `"no"` if not |
| `voted` | `1` if the person voted in 2006, `0` if not |

Run this box now. It loads the data and shows you the first few rows.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - ex_p1
#|   - ex_p2
#|   - ex_p3
voting <- read.csv("voting.csv")
```

```{webr}
#| startover: true
voting <- read.csv("voting.csv")
head(voting)
nrow(voting)
```

### One new thing, free of charge

A **data frame** is a table. You have not been taught these yet, and you do not
need to be. There is exactly one thing to know today:

```{webr}
#| startover: true
head(voting$voted)
```

The dollar sign pulls **one column out as a vector**. And a vector is exactly
what you spent all of last class learning to handle. `voting$voted` is a vector
of 229,444 zeros and ones; `voting$message` is a vector of `"yes"` and `"no"`.

One consequence worth pausing on. When a variable is coded 0/1, its **mean is a
proportion**:

```{webr}
#| startover: true
mean(voting$voted)
```

31% of everyone in the study voted. Hold onto that trick --- both problems below
depend on it.

## Problem 1. Who turned out? {.unnumbered}

[≈ 6 minutes]{.timing}

**Your question:** *Among the people who received the mailing, what share
voted?*

::: {.target}
**Target output.** Your code is right when the box prints exactly this:

```
[1] 0.3779482
```
:::

::: {.turn}
**Your turn.** Go to your LLM tab and ask for R code that answers the question.
Paste what it gives you into the box below and run it.

Write your prompt into the comment block first, so you can see it next to what
it produced.
:::

```{webr}
#| startover: true
#| exercise: ex_p1
# MY PROMPT:
# ______
#
# THE CODE IT GAVE ME:
______
```

::::: {.hint exercise="ex_p1"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Hint

Did your first attempt produce code referring to a column called `treatment`,
or `turnout`, or `group`? Of course it did. **The model cannot see your
screen.** It does not know your data exists.

Tell it: the data frame is called `voting`, the columns are `birth`, `message`
and `voted`, `message` is the text `"yes"` or `"no"`, and `voted` is `1` or `0`.

Then ask again.
:::
:::::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_p1"}
**Solution:**

```r
mean(voting$voted[voting$message == "yes"])
```

Read it from the inside out. `voting$message == "yes"` produces a vector of
`TRUE`/`FALSE`, one per person. Putting that inside `[ ]` keeps only the rows
where it is `TRUE`. Then `mean()` of a 0/1 vector gives the proportion who
voted: **0.378**, or about 38%.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The lesson of Problem 1

Almost nobody gets this on the first prompt, and the reason is always the same:
the first prompt described the *question* but not the *data*.

An LLM will never tell you it is guessing at your column names. It will write
confident, well-formatted, completely inapplicable code. Supplying the shape of
your data is not politeness --- it is the difference between an answer and a
fabrication.
:::

## Problem 2. Did the mailing work? {.unnumbered}

[≈ 7 minutes]{.timing}

This is the actual finding of the paper.

**Your question:** *How much higher was turnout among people who got the
mailing, compared with those who did not?*

::: {.target}
**Target output.** One number:

```
[1] 0.08130991
```
:::

::: {.turn}
**Your turn.** Same routine. But this time, before you paste anything, do one
extra thing: **say out loud how many separate steps this takes.** If your
prompt does not mention all of them, it will not work in one go.
:::

```{webr}
#| startover: true
#| exercise: ex_p2
# MY PROMPT:
# ______
#
# THE CODE IT GAVE ME:
______
```

::::: {.hint exercise="ex_p2"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Hint

Three steps, not one:

1. the turnout rate among people who got the mailing (you already have this),
2. the turnout rate among people who did not,
3. the difference between them.

A prompt that names all three gets working code. A prompt that says "find the
effect of the mailing" gets a regression, or a t-test, or a paragraph about
causal inference --- because "effect" is your word, not an instruction.
:::
:::::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_p2"}
**Solution:**

```r
treated <- mean(voting$voted[voting$message == "yes"])
control <- mean(voting$voted[voting$message == "no"])
treated - control
```

**0.081** --- an 8.1 percentage point increase in turnout. That is a very large
effect for a get-out-the-vote intervention, and it is the result the paper is
famous for.
:::

::: {.turn}
**Before you move on.** Pick any single line of the code you were given and
write, in the comment block, what it does in plain English. Not what it is
*for* --- what it *does*.

If you cannot, you do not have it yet. Ask the model to explain that one line,
then write the explanation in your own words.
:::

## Problem 3. Stretch {.unnumbered}

[If you have time --- otherwise, take it home]{.timing}

**Your question:** *Was the mailing more effective for older voters than for
younger ones?*

Split the sample at age 50 in 2006, and compute the effect from Problem 2
separately within each group.

::: {.target}
**Target output.** Two numbers --- age 50 and over first, then under 50:

```
[1] 0.08827899
[1] 0.07448951
```
:::

```{webr}
#| startover: true
#| exercise: ex_p3
# MY PROMPT:
# ______
#
# THE CODE IT GAVE ME:
______
```

::::: {.hint exercise="ex_p3"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Hint

There is no `age` column. You have `birth`, and the election was in 2006.

That is the whole difficulty: the thing you want to split on **does not exist
in the data yet**, and the model has no way of knowing you want it built. You
have to say so.
:::
:::::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_p3"}
**Solution:**

```r
age <- 2006 - voting$birth
old <- age >= 50

mean(voting$voted[old & voting$message == "yes"]) -
  mean(voting$voted[old & voting$message == "no"])

mean(voting$voted[!old & voting$message == "yes"]) -
  mean(voting$voted[!old & voting$message == "no"])
```

**8.8 points** for the over-50s against **7.4** for the under-50s. A real
difference, though a modest one next to the headline effect --- and now you have
a substantive question to argue about rather than a coding one.
:::

## What you just did {.unnumbered}

You loaded a 229,444-row dataset, subset it on a condition, computed group
means, and estimated a treatment effect --- in your third class, having been
taught none of it.

That is the honest case for these tools, and it is a strong one.

But notice **which parts the model could not do for you**:

- It did not know your data existed. You supplied that.
- It did not know "effect" meant a difference in means. You decided that.
- It did not know there was no age column. You noticed that.
- It could not tell you whether `0.378` was a sensible number. You checked that.

Every one of those is a judgement about *your* problem, and none of them get
easier by asking harder. This is why the research on novice programmers and AI
([Prather et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17739)) finds the tools help
students who already know what they are trying to do, and actively mislead the
students who do not. Code that runs feels like progress. It isn't, on its own.

::: {.rule}
**Keep this for the semester.**

1. Say what you want before you ask.
2. Give it your data --- names, coding, shape. It cannot see your screen.
3. Run it.
4. Check one number you can verify yourself.
5. If you cannot explain a line, you do not have it yet.
:::

**Next class --- Part II: Break It.** You will get R code that runs perfectly
and gives the wrong answer, with no error message anywhere. Rule 4 is the only
thing that saves you.
